trainerView:
Draft profile

Adults with no mental health training or caring role, from any setting, who want to notice distress in people around them and respond well. Their role is informal: listening, offering basic support and encouraging help-seeking; they are not expected to counsel, diagnose or manage a crisis alone.

Usually no training; some exposure through awareness campaigns, media or a one-off session.

They bring warmth and everyday relationships, but tend to give advice, minimise ("think positive"), or freeze when distress is serious, and may not know when or how to suggest further help.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: urban, peri-urban or rural; colleges, workplaces, neighbourhoods, faith or community groups, online.

Nature of the role · Typical: no role; voluntary participation.

Scope of practice · Confirm: notice distress, listen, offer basic support, encourage and help the person reach other help; counselling, diagnosis and managing risk alone are outside it.

Supervision · Typical: none.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: wide range, from school level to postgraduate.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: usually none; some exposure through awareness campaigns, media or a short workshop.

Work experience · Typical: not applicable; informal experience of supporting friends and family.

Past training experiences · Can be: none, or one-off awareness sessions or webinars.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: warmth, existing trust in relationships, being present in everyday moments.

What they struggle with · Confirm: knowing what to say, staying with someone's distress without fixing it, recognising when more help is needed, knowing where to point people.

Habitual responses · Typical: giving advice or solutions quickly; minimising or reassuring ("it'll be fine", "think positive"); turning to their own stories; avoiding the topic; using stigmatising words without meaning harm; pushing someone abruptly to "get treatment".
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: knowing what to say and do, and not making things worse.

As partners describe them · Typical: awareness, reduced stigma, more help-seeking.

Where these differ · Typical: learners want confidence in conversations; partners often measure awareness or reach.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position · Can be: anyone; peers of the people they support.

Stance on the role · Can be: motivated by personal experience, worry about someone close, or general interest.

Wellbeing · Typical: some carry their own or a loved one's experience of distress, so heavy content may land personally.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: varies; often a regional language, Hindi or English, with code-mixing.

Languages for learning · Confirm: the language they are most comfortable reading and speaking.

Literacy · Can be: wide range; short text works for most.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: own time, evenings and weekends; privacy for voice roleplays varies.

Draft profile

Family members, often women, supporting a relative at home with concerns ranging from distress to severe mental illness. Their role is to support and communicate with their relative and help them reach and stay with care; they are not expected to treat or manage a crisis alone.

Usually no training; some have had psychoeducation through a hospital, NGO or support group. Caring experience ranges from newly worried to many years.

They know their relative deeply and are committed, but often struggle with conflict, setting limits and their own exhaustion, and can fall into criticising, pleading or taking control.

Caring is usually long-term and unpaid, with stigma and family pressures shaping what they can say and do.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: urban or rural; at home; connected to a hospital, NGO or caregiver support group, or not connected to services.

Nature of the role · Typical: unpaid, ongoing caring alongside work and household duties; often mothers, wives and daughters.

Scope of practice · Confirm: emotional support, communicating with their relative, encouraging and accompanying them to care, supporting treatment, noticing warning signs; diagnosing, treating and managing a crisis alone are outside it.

Supervision · Typical: none; some have a support group or a treating team they can contact.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: wide range.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: usually none; some psychoeducation from a treating team or support group.

Work experience · Confirm: from newly worried to many years of caring.

Past training experiences · Can be: none, or psychoeducation sessions or support group meetings.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: knowledge of their relative, commitment, persistence, practical support.

What they struggle with · Confirm: communicating without conflict; responding to anger, withdrawal or unusual beliefs; setting limits; looking after themselves; handling stigma from others.

Habitual responses · Typical: criticising, blaming or arguing; pleading or giving ultimatums; over-protecting or taking control; minimising ("it's just stress"); hiding the problem from others.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: how to talk to their relative, what to do in difficult moments, how to cope themselves.

As partners describe them · Typical: treatment adherence, fewer relapses, calmer home environments, caregiver wellbeing.

Where these differ · Typical: caregivers often ask for support for themselves; partners tend to focus on the relative's outcomes.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position · Typical: insiders in the person's life; may face stigma themselves.

Stance on the role · Can be: committed, exhausted, ambivalent, or feeling blamed.

Wellbeing · Typical: high caregiver strain, grief and isolation; heavy content may mirror their own home.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: the family's home language; often a regional language or Hindi, English for some.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the home language.

Literacy · Can be: wide range; audio and video help many.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: short, often interrupted time at home; privacy may be limited, especially for roleplays close to their own situation.

trainerView:
Draft profile

Volunteers and peer supporters, often women and often with lived experience, working in villages, small towns and peri-urban settlements through NGOs, collectives or community programmes. They listen, offer emotional support and link people to services; they are not expected to counsel, diagnose or manage risk alone.

Usually a short NGO-run training of a few days; experience varies, and turnover can be high.

They are trusted locally and speak the community's language, but often find it hard to listen without advising, keep confidences in close-knit settings, and respond to suicide risk or violence.

They share the community's social position, including caste, gender and economic pressures, which shapes both trust and risk.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: villages, small towns, peri-urban settlements; through NGOs, self-help groups, collectives or community programmes.

Nature of the role · Typical: volunteers, sometimes with a small stipend; part-time alongside other work.

Scope of practice · Confirm: listening, emotional support, basic information about mental health, linking people to health, social and legal services, follow-up; counselling, diagnosis and managing risk alone are outside it.

Supervision · Can be: NGO field coordinators or community facilitators; often irregular.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: often school level; varies widely.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: a short NGO training, often a few days; some exposure to other programmes such as health, rights or livelihoods.

Work experience · Confirm: wide range; volunteer turnover can be high.

Past training experiences · Typical: in-person group sessions, often participatory.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: trust and access, shared language and experience, knowing local services and people.

What they struggle with · Confirm: listening without advising or solving, confidentiality in close communities, boundaries, responding to suicide risk, violence or severe distress.

Habitual responses · Typical: giving advice or solutions; reassuring quickly; involving family or elders by default; moralising; sharing their own story at length.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: skills to help the people they already support, and recognition for the work.

As partners describe them · Typical: identifying people in distress, emotional support, linking to services.

Where these differ · Typical: learners may want support for themselves and for heavy cases; partners may focus on reach and linkage numbers.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position · Typical: insiders who share the community's social position, which brings trust and exposure to the same pressures.

Stance on the role · Can be: motivated by lived experience, service or standing in the community; at risk of being stretched thin.

Wellbeing · Typical: may face the same hardships as those they support; strain from cases involving violence or suicide.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: regional language and local dialect.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the same.

Literacy · Confirm: wide range; audio and video preferred.

Draft profile

Volunteers and peer supporters in cities and towns, often young adults or people with lived experience, supporting others through NGOs, campuses, workplaces or online communities. They listen, offer peer support and point people to services; they are not expected to counsel, diagnose or manage a crisis alone.

Usually a short listening or peer support training; some have a psychology background. Many are new to the role.

They are open about mental health and use shared experience well, but may over-identify, share their own story too much, or slip into popular therapy language, and find boundaries and risk hard.

Often motivated by lived experience; burnout is a risk where peer roles have little structure.

trainerView:
Draft profile

People who answer mental health, emotional support or crisis helplines by phone or chat, from trained volunteers on shifts to paid tele-counsellors. They listen, assess risk using the helpline's protocol, offer brief support and connect callers to services; ongoing counselling is usually outside their role.

Usually helpline-specific training on listening, risk and protocols, with supervised early calls; paid responders may hold psychology or social work degrees.

They are used to talking with strangers in distress and to following protocol, but may sound scripted, rush to risk questions or problem-solving, and find silence, angry or repeat callers, and voice-only cues hard.

High, repeated exposure to suicide and crisis calls, often on shifts.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: NGO-run or government helplines; phone, chat or both; remote or call-centre based.

Nature of the role · Can be: trained volunteers on shifts, or paid full- or part-time tele-counsellors.

Scope of practice · Confirm: listening, brief emotional support, risk assessment by protocol, safety planning where trained, connecting callers to services; ongoing counselling is usually outside it.

Supervision · Typical: shift supervisors or on-call seniors; debriefs after difficult calls, which vary in practice.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: volunteers vary; paid responders often have a bachelor's or master's in psychology or social work.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: helpline-specific training, often several days plus supervised calls.

Work experience · Confirm: wide range; volunteer turnover can be high.

Past training experiences · Typical: protocol-based training with roleplays and shadowing.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: staying calm with strangers in distress, following protocol, asking directly about suicide.

What they struggle with · Confirm: sounding natural rather than scripted; silence; angry, abusive or repeat callers; building rapport without visual cues; ending calls well.

Habitual responses · Typical: moving quickly to scripted questions or risk checklists; problem-solving or advising early; over-reassuring; filling silences; ending calls abruptly under time pressure.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: handling difficult calls and their own after-effects.

As partners describe them · Typical: consistent protocol adherence, sound risk assessment, call quality.

Where these differ · Typical: learners want support with emotional load; partners focus on protocol and quality.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position or professional identity · Can be: volunteers with a service identity, or early-career professionals.

Stance on the role · Typical: committed, under strain from crisis-heavy work.

Wellbeing · Typical: high exposure to suicide and crisis; vicarious trauma and burnout are real risks.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: Hindi, English and regional languages, depending on the helpline.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the helpline's main language.

Literacy · Typical: moderate to high.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: between calls or outside shifts; shared call-centre space can limit privacy.

They are trusted insiders with good access to families, but may find non-directive emotional support hard and tend to advise or reassure quickly.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: any state or district, rural or urban.

Nature of the role · Typical: often women; designated honorary volunteers paid a fixed monthly amount plus task-based incentives, not a salary.

Scope of practice · Confirm: identify, offer basic support, refer, follow up. Not expected to diagnose or provide counselling.

Supervision · Can be: ASHA facilitators, ANMs or PHC medical officers; mental health work often has no dedicated supervision.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: may be up to Class 8–10.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: often training focused on health; little or no mental health training.

Work experience · Confirm: wide range; many long-serving workers alongside recent recruits.

Past training experiences · Typical: classroom-style training at block or PHC level.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: trusted access to households, knowledge of families and local context, navigating the public health system, persistent follow-up.

What they struggle with · Confirm: telling distress from illness, gaps in understanding causes and treatment, opening conversations about mental health, time, providing non-directive emotional support.

Habitual responses · Typical: advising or reassuring quickly ("don't think too much"); bringing in family by default, which risks breaching confidentiality; moving fast to referral or medication; using the same stigmatising language as the community.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: interest in more mental health training and periodic refreshers.

As partners describe them · Typical: case identification, referral and treatment adherence.

Where these differ · Typical: learners may also want help with conversations and their own load.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position · Typical: insiders from the community they serve, which brings trust and also shared beliefs about mental illness and social pressure on confidentiality.

Stance on the role · Typical: mental health may feel like another unpaid duty; ongoing collective action over pay and workload in several states.

Wellbeing · Typical: own exposure to distress, gender-based violence and work strain, as it bears on emotionally heavy content.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: state language and local dialect.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the same.

Literacy · Confirm: functional reading in the regional language; short text, with audio and video preferred.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: between field visits, evenings, or at monthly PHC meetings; little privacy at home for speaking voice roleplays aloud.

trainerView:
Draft profile

Frontline staff in sectors next to mental health (child protection, gender-based violence, disability, livelihoods, migration, harm reduction, policing) who meet people in distress as part of their main work. Their mental health role is to respond supportively, recognise distress and risk, and link people to services; they are not expected to counsel or treat.

Training is mostly in their own sector, with little or no mental health training, though social workers may have some.

They are skilled at practical help and navigating systems, but may move straight to procedures, questioning or fixing, and find it hard to stay with distress, especially after trauma.

Heavy caseloads and repeated exposure to violence and crisis; their institutional role, such as enforcement, can shape how people respond to them.

fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: NGOs, government departments and schemes, police stations, one-stop centres, community field work; urban or rural.

Nature of the role · Typical: paid staff, often full-time; some on contracts.

Scope of practice · Confirm: a supportive first response, recognising distress and risk, psychological first aid, linking people to mental health and other services; counselling and treatment are outside it.

Supervision · Can be: line managers or case supervisors; focused on cases and compliance more than emotional support.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: from school level (outreach workers) to MSW or other degrees.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: sector-specific training; little or no mental health training; social work graduates may have some.

Work experience · Confirm: wide range.

Past training experiences · Typical: sector trainings and orientations, often lecture-based.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: practical help, knowledge of entitlements and systems, persistence, managing crises logistically.

What they struggle with · Confirm: staying with distress, trauma-informed responses, not retraumatising during questioning, recognising mental health needs behind the presenting problem.

Habitual responses · Typical: moving quickly to forms, procedures or fact-finding; questioning in ways that feel like interrogation; giving instructions; reassuring that "everything will be handled"; doubting or testing disclosures.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: handling distressed people and difficult disclosures; looking after themselves.

As partners describe them · Typical: trauma-informed practice, better identification and linkage.

Where these differ · Typical: learners want help with emotional load; partners focus on case outcomes.
5. Attitudes and context

Professional identity · Typical: tied to their sector and its mandate; mental health may feel outside their job.

Stance on the role · Can be: committed, or doubtful that mental health is part of their work.

Wellbeing · Typical: high exposure to violence, trauma and crisis; vicarious trauma and burnout are common.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: regional language or Hindi; English for some.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the working language.

Draft profile

Psychiatrists and psychiatry residents in hospitals, district programmes, private practice and telepsychiatry, often with very high outpatient volumes. They diagnose, prescribe and lead treatment, and may provide or supervise psychotherapy depending on their training.

A medical degree and psychiatry specialisation; psychotherapy training varies widely.

They are expert in diagnosis, medication and risk, but may hold brief, symptom-focused consultations and find longer, person-led conversations and shared decision-making hard.

High volumes and medical hierarchy; their authority shapes how patients and families speak with them.
Questions

Does this profile fit your learners? Edit anything that's off, especially their stage (residents or consultants), psychotherapy training, and what they do well or struggle with.

Which languages do they use with patients and families, and which should the course and roleplays use?

Optional: where do they mostly work? (teaching hospital · general or district hospital · private practice · telepsychiatry)
fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Confirm: teaching hospitals, general or district hospitals, district programmes, private practice, telepsychiatry.

Nature of the role · Typical: paid, usually full-time.

Scope of practice · Confirm: diagnosis, prescribing, risk assessment, admission decisions and leading treatment; psychotherapy depending on training.

Supervision · Can be: consultants supervise residents; consultants rely on peers.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: MBBS plus a psychiatry specialisation; residents in training.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: psychiatry training; psychotherapy training varies from none to formal.

Work experience · Confirm: from residents to senior consultants.

Past training experiences · Typical: continuing medical education, conferences, academic teaching.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: diagnosis, pharmacology, managing risk, working across systems.

What they struggle with · Confirm: time, shared decision-making, exploring psychosocial context, communicating with families.

Habitual responses · Typical: symptom checklists and closed questions; directive advice; reassurance; focusing on medication.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: brief psychotherapeutic skills and communication that fit short consultations.

As partners describe them · Typical: quality of care and patient experience.

Where these differ · Typical: learners want efficient tools; partners want better engagement and experience.
5. Attitudes and context

Professional identity · Typical: a strong medical identity; may see communication training as basic.

Stance on the role · Can be: interested in psychotherapy, or focused on biomedical treatment.

Wellbeing · Typical: high volumes and burnout.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: local languages with patients and families; English in clinical work.

Languages for learning · Typical: English, with roleplays in patients' language where needed.

Literacy · Typical: high.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: short gaps or after hours; usually some privacy.

name: Supervisors and trainers
matching:
Region: India

Summary: People who supervise, mentor or train lay and frontline workers, such as ASHA facilitators, NGO field supervisors, lay counsellor supervisors and master trainers.

Matches when the trainer says: supervisors, field supervisors, ASHA facilitators, master trainers, trainers of trainers, programme coordinators, cluster coordinators, peer supervisors, mentors.

Nearest neighbours:

16. Senior counsellors, psychologists and therapists: if they supervise professionals clinically, use 16.

The group they supervise (e.g. 6 or 11): if they mainly do the frontline work themselves, use that entry.
trainerView:
Draft profile

Supervisors, mentors and trainers of lay and frontline workers, such as ASHA facilitators, NGO field coordinators, lay counsellor supervisors and master trainers in cascade programmes. Their role is to build and support others' skills, review practice, give feedback and handle escalations; some also do frontline work.

Often promoted from frontline roles, or with a social work or psychology background; little formal training in supervision.

They know the work and the workers well, but may supervise by checking targets or correcting, and find it hard to give specific, skill-based feedback or to support workers emotionally.

They sit between programme management and frontline workers, carrying pressure from both.
Questions

Does this profile fit your learners? Edit anything that's off, especially whom they supervise or train, their background and experience, and what they do well or struggle with.

Which language should the course use, and how comfortable are learners reading it?

Optional: who supports them in this role? (programme manager · specialist clinician · no one)
fullProfile:
1. Role and work

Setting · Can be: NGOs and public health programmes, at block or district level; field visits and meetings.

Nature of the role · Typical: paid; part of a programme hierarchy.

Scope of practice · Confirm: supervision, feedback on practice, training delivery, case review and escalation, supporting workers' wellbeing.

Supervision · Can be: programme managers or specialist clinicians; sometimes no one.
2. Background

Education · Confirm: from school level (promoted frontline workers) to MSW or psychology degrees.

Prior relevant training · Confirm: training in the content they supervise; little in supervision or giving feedback.

Work experience · Confirm: often experienced in the frontline role.

Past training experiences · Typical: cascade trainings and trainings of trainers, often lecture-based.
3. Current practice

What they do well · Confirm: knowing the work and the workers, practical problem-solving, programme knowledge.

What they struggle with · Confirm: specific, skill-based feedback, observing practice, supportive supervision, modelling skills.

Habitual responses · Typical: checking records and targets; correcting or instructing; telling rather than drawing out; lecturing in trainings; taking over cases.
4. Learning needs

As learners report them · Typical: how to give feedback and support struggling workers.

As partners describe them · Typical: quality and fidelity of frontline work.

Where these differ · Typical: learners want help with the people side; partners focus on quality and targets.
5. Attitudes and context

Community position or professional identity · Typical: in the middle, accountable upward and responsible downward; often from the same community as the workers.

Stance on the role · Can be: proud of a mentoring role, or seeing it as monitoring.

Wellbeing · Typical: carrying workers' distress and programme pressure.
6. Language and communication

Languages at work · Confirm: regional language; English for some.

Languages for learning · Confirm: usually the working language.

Literacy · Can be: moderate to high.
7. Learning access

When and where they learn · Typical: around field visits and meetings; privacy varies.
